implementation_notes: Since Java 11 the JDK ships both roles: a shared java.net.http.HttpClient is the connection - connection pool, HTTP/2, redirect policy, proxy and authenticator configured once on its builder - and the gateway is a small class holding it that returns domestic types. Asynchronous methods are built from sendAsync, which returns CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<T>>, so independent remote calls compose without blocking a thread; choose the blocking send when the flow is a simple request/response already running on a worker thread (or inside a virtual thread). Translation is explicit: map JSON with Jackson/Gson into your own records and turn status codes, HttpTimeoutException and IOException into the domestic exception type.
pitfalls: An HttpClient is immutable and pools connections: constructing one per request throws the pool away, while closing a shared client (Java 21 close()) breaks calls already in flight.

sendAsync runs dependent stages on the client's executor, which defaults to the common ForkJoinPool: blocking work inside thenApply can starve unrelated tasks - supply an executor or use virtual threads deliberately.
HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString() buffers the whole body; large or streaming responses need a stream handler, and unread streams can prevent an orderly shutdown from completing.
HttpClient throws only for transport-level problems and timeouts; a 404 or 500 is a normal response, so status translation is the gateway's job.

variants.name: JDBC Connection/PreparedStatement table data gateway
variants.implementation_notes: The book-era Java realization for relational resources: one class owns all the SQL for a table or data source and exposes find/insert/update methods in domestic terms; java.sql.PreparedStatement binds parameters (never string-concatenated SQL), the ResultSet rows are mapped into records, and SQLException is translated into the application's data-access exception. Inject a javax.sql.DataSource (or Connection) so the gateway gets a pooled connection and tests can pass a fake; try-with-resources guarantees statements and result sets are closed. Keep this shape when the external system is a database accessed with SQL - it is the table data gateway form - and prefer the HTTP client when the foreign system is a service.
pitfalls: A JDBC Connection is single-threaded and must not be shared across threads; acquire one per call or per transaction from the DataSource instead of caching it in a field.
Never build SQL by string concatenation - that is the injection bug the PreparedStatement exists to prevent.
Vendor error codes and SQLState values differ between drivers: translate SQLException without pattern-matching on the message text.
Reading only part of a ResultSet without closing it (or fetching without a tuned fetchSize) leaks cursors and memory on large tables.
